speaker: skiff
lines: You're the bird from up the valley. Nana's girl.
Look at this. Three feet of ice and no water to float a boat.
I've got a sled up in the rafters. Been there since the freeze. Nobody rides it.

speaker: skiff
lines: An otter with a boat in a field. That's what.
The pike are down there somewhere. Sitting in the dark, laughing at me.
I know where they sit. Ask me later if you need to find them.

speaker: skiff
lines: Then find Margit, the raven who counts the ice. She's out there now.
Ask her if it'll hold a sled. And don't let her talk your ear off.

speaker: pip
lines: a sled nobody rides.
and a raven who counts ice.

speaker: skiff
lines: Ask the raven, Margit, if the ice holds. She's precise about it.
Then come back and tell me.

speaker: skiff
lines: Then ask the raven, Margit, if the ice holds a sled.

speaker: skiff
lines: So the raven says it holds. Good enough for me.
Then mine comes down off the roof. Here. Not a loan: yours, on any slope you like.
Use it hard. That's all a sled wants. Same as a boat.

speaker: skiff
lines: Margit, the raven, wants my pike spot? She sent you to ask me?
Fine. Off the end of the old jetty, where the bottom drops away.
They sit there all winter in the dark. Don't tell anyone else.
And tell her I said to write it down right.

speaker: skiff
lines: Flour for Orla, up at the bakery? Aye, it's in the hold.
Boat's frozen in, but the hold's dry. Three sacks, sealed in oilcloth.
I'll haul them up the hill by sled this evening. Tell her that.
And tell her I'll want the first loaf. Captain's due.

speaker: skiff
lines: Still no water. Still a captain. Somebody has to be.
Ride that sled for me. It's been waiting longer than I have.
Come spring, I'll take you out on real water. You'll see.

speaker: margit
lines: The ice is forty-one centimetres at the centre. Forty-three at the edge.
The otter with the boat, Skiff, calls that luck. I call it a measurement.
I'm counting today. You fish. Bring me something worth writing down.

speaker: margit
lines: Because the lake doesn't lie. People do. Numbers don't.
Skiff thinks the ice insulted him. I think it's a record.
Go on. The hole's drilled. I'll count while you pull.

speaker: margit
lines: Fish the hole. I'll count the minutes. Whatever bites, I'll write it down.
Then ask the otter with the boat, Skiff, where the pike sit.
He knows. He just won't say it out loud. Not to me.

speaker: margit
lines: You're back. The hole's still open, and I'm still counting.
Fish it. Then get Skiff to tell you where the pike sit.

speaker: margit
lines: Fish the hole. I'm counting. Then ask the otter, Skiff, where the pike sit.

speaker: margit
lines: Here's the good bait. Use it off the jetty. Then bring me the next number.

speaker: margit
lines: Skiff, the otter with the boat, wants to know if it holds a sled?
Forty-one centimetres at the centre. It would hold Skiff and his boat.
Tell him yes. Tell him it's a measurement, not luck.
And tell him to stop sulking at the lake. It doesn't notice.

speaker: margit
lines: It's forty-one at the centre, forty-three at the edge. Same as yesterday.
Same is good. Same is a record holding.
Fish if you like. I'll count. I always count.

speaker: orla
lines: You must be Pip. Sit down, you look frozen through.
The oven's on, but I've no flour. Skiff, the otter with the boat, has it.
Would you ask him for me?

choices.text: why is flour on a boat?

speaker: orla
lines: Skiff ferries it up the lake each autumn. This year the ice won.
So the sacks sit in his hold, frozen in, and my oven eats wood.
He'll know if any of it's dry. Ask nicely. He sulks about that boat.

speaker: orla
lines: Skiff's boat is iced in, down on the Frozen Reach. He'll know what's aboard.

speaker: pip
lines: flour in a boat, frozen in. poor oven.

speaker: orla
lines: No flour? Skiff's telling you about the one that got away, I expect.
Take your time. The oven's holding.

speaker: orla
lines: The flour's coming? Tonight? Then the oven stays on.
And there's a snowman on the green, leaning at my window. Yours, I'd bet. It's just right.
Here. Two tins of soup. One for you, one for Nana.
And Skiff wants the first loaf, does he? He'll get it. Thank you, love.

speaker: orla
lines: Corm, the raven, says we're closed? I've been open since five.
Flour or no flour, the oven's lit. That's open.
Tell him to come and eat something. Then tell him to check his facts.

speaker: orla
lines: Which house is blue? Mine. Look at the door. I painted it in spring.
Pell asks me this every winter. Then he asks somebody else.
Tell him the bakery. Blue door, flour on the step. He can't miss it.

speaker: orla
lines: I've lit the market lamps for a night bake. Four loaves won't feed this queue.
I'd like a picture of the lamps for the window. And a bell rung when the bread's out.
Gus, who sells bells across the square, has the loudest one. Borrow him for an hour.

speaker: orla
lines: He's loud. People hear the bell and know the bread's out.
He'll talk your ear off, but he'll do it.

speaker: orla
lines: Then go and get Gus from his shop, and his bell.
Then come back and tell me the queue's fed.

speaker: orla
lines: Then go and get Gus from the bell shop, with his bell.

speaker: orla
lines: Then go and get Gus from the bell shop, with his loud bell.

speaker: orla
lines: Nine loaves. The queue's fed.
You take the credit. I'm going to sit down for five minutes.
Thank you, Pip. Really.

speaker: orla
lines: Nine loaves one day, four the next. Somewhere in between is right.
Sit down, Pip. You look frozen through. There's always a heel of bread.
Tell Nana there's a loaf here whenever she wants one.

speaker: pell
lines: I've one letter left in the bag, and it's been in there a week.
It says 'The blue house, road head.' I've four blue houses on my round.
I numbered them. It didn't help.

speaker: pell
lines: Paint fades up here. Frost takes the blue first, then it all goes grey.
So four doors that were blue once. And only one letter.
Nana's cabin at the road head is my best guess. Take it and ask.

speaker: pell
lines: Take the letter down to Hearth Hollow. Give it to Nana at the cabin.
Into her hands, mind. Not the step. Then I'll sleep.

speaker: pip
lines: a blue door at the road head.
nana's is blue.

speaker: pell
lines: Still got it? Nana's cabin is in Hearth Hollow, at the road head.
Into her hands. That's all I ask.

speaker: pell
lines: You gave it to Nana? And it was the right house?
One letter. One correct delivery. I'll take that.
By her stove, she's keeping it? That's where good letters go. A job done right.

speaker: pell
lines: Gus, the bell-seller, wants to know how far his shop bell carries?
I heard it ring, from the far end of my round. Clean.
It carries the whole hamlet. Every door I knocked, it got there first.
Tell him the whole hamlet. He'll go pink. Let him.

speaker: pell
lines: Is the post running? Corm, the raven, sent you to ask? Typical.
Inside the valley, yes. I walk it every morning, door to door.
Over the pass, no. Nothing goes over till the road's cleared.
Tell him both halves. He only ever repeats one.

speaker: pell
lines: That letter found Nana by luck. The next one might not.
Orla, the mouse with the bakery, knows every door in the hamlet. Ask her which house is blue.
Ivy, the otter who keeps the springs, sees the whole hill from below. Ask her too.

speaker: pell
lines: Ivy sees every house on the hill from the pools. That's her post, in a way.
Orla sees every door from her counter. Between them, they've the whole round.

speaker: pell
lines: Ask Orla which house is blue. Ask Ivy, at the springs, too.
Then come back. I'll have the ledger open.

speaker: pell
lines: You're back. The ledger's open. Which house is blue?
Ask Orla, at the bakery, first. Then Ivy, down at Kettle Springs.

speaker: pell
lines: Ask Orla, at the bakery, which house is blue. Then Ivy, at the springs. I'll keep the ledger open.

speaker: pell
lines: Orla says her door. Ivy says the green one, from where she sits.
Two answers. Both right, from where they stand. No use to a postmaster.
So I'll stop writing colours. I'll write names. Everyone knows a name.
Thank you, Pip. I can sleep now.

speaker: pell
lines: Names on the front now, not colours. Not one letter astray since.
Turns out everybody knows where everybody lives. I only had to ask.
Mind the step. I've sanded it, but it's sneaky.

speaker: gus
lines: I sell bells. Every size. And I've never once heard the big one ring.
My shop bell, though. One clean strike, and I want to know how far it goes.
Pell, the postmaster, walks the whole hamlet. Ask him if he heard it.

choices.text: why not ring the big bell?

speaker: gus
lines: It's the biggest bell in the valley! Nobody's rung it in years.
What if I pull the rope and it goes clunk? In front of everyone?
So. The shop bell first. If that carries, maybe the big one will.

speaker: gus
lines: Then ask Pell how far the sound travelled. He'll know. He hears every door.

speaker: gus
lines: Then ask Pell, out on his round, how far it carried.

speaker: gus
lines: Then ask Pell, the postmaster, how far it carried.

speaker: gus
lines: It carries the hamlet? The whole hamlet?
Then the big bell could reach the valley. I've got to try it. Soon. Fairly soon.
Here, take these. Bells for your trouble. Spend them on my feathers. They buy you breath.

speaker: gus
lines: Orla, at the bakery, wants me? For an hour? To ring?
I'll ring for bread any day. Loaves out, bell rings, queue comes.
Lock the shop? No. Nobody steals bells. They'd be heard.
Tell her I'm on my way. Bringing the loud one.

speaker: gus
lines: Bells! Bells for sale! ...Oh, it's you. Hello.
I'm working up to the big bell. I've held the rope. That's a start.
One day I'll pull it, and the whole valley will hear. You'll see.
Those two feathers by my feet are forty bells each. Longer breath for the climb.
